papers.title: A site-resolved post-translational modification framework for drug-response analysis
papers.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate protein activity and treatment-associated signalling, providing functional information that can connect drug-response estimates with candidate pharmacodynamic measurements. Assessing this information requires a framework that determines its contribution beyond fixed molecular features while retaining the identity of the modified sites underlying model predictions. We developed the PTM Biological Dynamics Layer (PTM-BDL), which integrates typed PTM states with protein sequence, structure-derived and drug chemical features to predict log-transformed half-maximal inhibitory concentration and resistance while providing site-level interpretation through integrated gradients. Retrospective evaluation used source-derived and propagated PTM profiles across biologically distinct BCR-ABL, HDAC/EP300 and EGFR/ERBB2 settings, yielding internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) between 0.785 and 0.946. Retraining demonstrated a consistent incremental contribution from PTM inputs in K562/CML, with a mean AUROC increase of 0.0268 and positive gains in all five folds, alongside more modest incremental gains in HeLa/HDAC and EGFR/ERBB2. Within K562/CML, CRKL Y207 and STAT5A Y694 retained the leading attribution ranks for their proteins across three seeds, while greater PTM attribution in dasatinib than in cytotoxic drug contexts identified a focused setting for pharmacodynamic investigation. These findings support context-dependent use of PTM information and connect predictive assessment with prioritisation of individual sites, providing a basis for targeted pharmacodynamic measurements and independent experimental validation.

papers.title: MSGFLEX: An optimized end-to-end pipeline for proteomics and metaproteomics analysis built on MS-GF+ with a dedicated rescoring model XPECTRA
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics workflows often face competing demands between identification sensitivity, false discovery rate (FDR) control, and computational scalability, particularly for metaproteomic datasets that require searching large and complex sequence databases. Here, we present MSGFLEX, an integrated end-to-end workflow that combines database searching, machine-learning based rescoring, and peptide-to-protein quantitative inference. MSGFLEX integrates three components: SPARX handles raw file conversion, and MS-GF+ database searching; XPECTRA is a cross-validated XGBoost ensemble that rescores peptide-spectrum matches by combining ensemble predictions with MS-GF+ search evidence through noisy-OR fusion model. QUANTIX provides protein quantification through multiple protein rollup strategies. Across four benchmarking datasets, XPECTRA consistently increased peptide and protein identifications relative to Percolator, MS2Rescore, and MSBooster. On a human gut metaproteome dataset, XPECTRA achieved the largest effect size among all methods evaluated (Cohen's d = 0.95; p < 0.0005). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based analysis indicated that XPECTRA learned consistent relationships from spectral and physicochemical features. Database partitioning does not introduce detectable bias in peptide identification or FDR estimation, while QUANTIX's DWrollup provides the most accurate recovery of known protein abundance changes in a ground-truth spike-in benchmark. Together, these results establish MSGFLEX as a scalable and interpretable framework for mass-spectrometry based proteomics and metaproteomics.

papers.title: Systematic inference of biological relatedness across the global ancient DNA record
papers.abstract: The rapidly expanding scale of ancient DNA data creates an increasing need for high-performance software methods. One area for such improvement is the inference of pairwise biological relatedness, a prominent aspect of many ancient DNA studies. We present fastpmr, a fast and memory-efficient method for biological relatedness inference based on the computation of pairwise mismatch rates. We demonstrate that fastpmr can achieve over 1000x speed-up over READv2, a widely used relatedness-inference method. We leverage this performance to investigate relatedness at the scale of the global ancient DNA record. Analyzing biological relatedness across all pairs in the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (n = 19,118 ancient and 23,089 total samples) recapitulates human evolutionary history and identifies previously unknown genetic duplicates and likely sample mix-ups, demonstrating fastpmr's utility for ancient DNA analysis and quality control at scale.

papers.title: Curated annotations locate biological concepts in protein language models from layers to neurons
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods describe what a network has learned, yet their claims are rarely tested against model-independent ground truth. We argue that proteins are an ideal modality for interpretability since curators annotate functional sites residue by residue. Across three ESMC protein language models (300M-6B parameters), we show that conclusions depend on where models are read, how concepts are decoded, which units are examined, and how they are scored. Concepts become linearly readable along depth long before erasure impairs masked-token prediction, and 20-fold scaling shifts concept depth more than peak score. Most of a nonlinear probe's lead over a linear one reflects fitting and readout shape rather than nonlinear encoding. Over whole proteins, saturated metrics render feed-forward neurons indistinguishable from random rotations. At annotated residues, dual-signed neuron poles identify 2.5-5.4 times as many concepts as rotations without training, though sparse autoencoders identify more. Without held-out validation, however, shuffled annotations label nearly every latent, and causal reliance emerges in neuron groups rather than single poles. Reading selected intra-block states exposes binding and active sites that stream probes read poorly and lifts a simple probe 5% above the best published MCC on a leakage-controlled interaction benchmark. We recommend reading a model directly against annotation, scoring units where they fire with a measure that is not saturated, and training a dictionary only where it adds coverage.

papers.title: PhageLysClass: Evidence-aware classification of phage lytic proteins using protein language models
papers.abstract: Phage lytic proteins are promising antibacterial and biotechnological candidates, yet uncertain annotations, modular architectures, and class imbalance complicate sequence-based classification. We developed PhageLysClass, an evidence-aware framework for recognizing lytic proteins and distinguishing Endolysins, Depolymerases, and virion-associated lytic enzymes. From 442,329 unique phage sequences, including 11,867 evidence-supported positives, we defined distinct candidate non-target, unlabeled, and challenge populations. Seven supervised and two positive-unlabeled tasks were evaluated across factorial redundancy and train-test homology conditions, yielding 2,240 and 768 experiments, respectively. Redundancy reduction influenced generalization more strongly than homology separation, with non-additive interactions between them. ESM2-T30 consistently outperformed alternative representations and supported a hierarchical classifier achieving approximately 0.89 MCC under strict R30/S30 conditions in the selected, pre-refitting benchmark. Applied without retraining to 77,897 sequences across three collections, PhageLysClass combined predictions with physicochemical and geometric contextualization, highlighting Depolymerase-like candidates among structurally ambiguous proteins while distinguishing reference-supported assignments from extrapolation.

papers.title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

papers.title: VEGABrain: a Visualizer of Enriched Gene Analysis for the developing human brain
papers.abstract: RNA sequencing datasets are widely reused resources in developmental neuroscience, yet inspecting them spatially remains unclear and difficult. Here, we present VEGABrain, an openly accessible web tool that renders bulk RNA-seq onto brain cortical and subcortical atlas surfaces across five human developmental windows spanning the first trimester to adulthood. Beyond single-gene maps, VEGABrain contributes a composite per-region enrichment layer using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) scores precomputed for [~]19,000 gene sets drawn from Gene Ontology, Reactome, KEGG, BioCarta, the Human Phenotype Ontology and the MSigDB hallmark collection, and aggregated to a score for every gene set, developmental window and brain region. Furthermore, VEGABrain allows users to submit a custom gene list and obtain its ssGSEA map across development, computed on demand. VEGABrain is open source and requires no installation, offering easy-to-query expression throughout development and brain areas.

papers.title: scPACE: A Personalized Autoencoder for Cell Evolution in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Single-cell studies increasingly profile large cohorts of individuals, measuring thousands of cells in each donor. These datasets contain information at two levels: variation among individual cells and among donors. Analyzing both levels requires methods that can learn cellular representations, infer cell and donor states, and account for cell types that may be missing in some donors. Existing methods partially address these tasks. We introduce scPACE, a hierarchical personalized variational autoencoder handling these tasks. scPACE learns a cell representation, a cell state, and then aggregates cells within each type of cell to infer a donor state. It also imputes missing cell types with confidence estimates. Across simulated cohorts and a developing mouse visual-cortex dataset, scPACE recovered held-out cell and donor states accurately while achieving efficient cell-type imputation and representation. scPACE provides a unified framework for learning phenotypes across cellular and donor scales in cohort-scale single-cell transcriptomics.

papers.title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
papers.abstract: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

papers.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

papers.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
papers.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

papers.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
papers.abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

papers.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
papers.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

papers.title: ARC-Impute: robust reference-guided spatial gene imputation through regularised cell-to-spot mapping
papers.abstract: Motivation: Reference-guided spatial imputation uses single-cell RNA sequencing references to predict genes that are unmeasured in spatial transcriptomics data. Limited shared-gene overlap can leave the mapping of reference cells to spatial locations ambiguous: different assignments may reconstruct observed genes similarly yet yield different imputed expression and cell-type estimates. This gives rise to local assignment ambiguity, source-target mismatch and reference-transfer instability. Results: We present ARC-Impute, which regularises cell-to-spot mapping through anchor-residual optimisation, target-guided reference curation and routing, and twin-panel consistency. Across 17 human and mouse datasets spanning spot-based and single-cell technologies, ARC-Impute ranked first for held-out Pearson correlation throughout and exceeded the dataset-specific baseline mean by 47.3% on average. It also achieved the strongest spot-level cell-type composition recovery across three pseudospot benchmarks and retained leading accuracy and consistency under reference and training-gene perturbations. Cross-validated predictions revealed systematic differences in gene imputability. Availability and implementation: Code and workflows at https://github.com/ethanhaan/arc-impute.

papers.title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
papers.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

papers.title: Haplotype reconstruction in multi-generational diploid and tetraploid populations
papers.abstract: Previously, we developed a statistical framework and software (PolyOrigin1) to reconstruct parental haplotypes of each offspring in connected tetraploid F1 populations. A key application of the technology is quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping, via regression of phenotypes on posterior probabilities of parental origins. In this work, we extend the methodology and software (PolyOrigin2) to multi-generational populations (both diploid and tetraploid), which are common in breeding programs. The extension links parental origins across generations to estimate posterior probabilities of founder origins. Compared to PolyOrigin1, the main challenge is to phase intermediate individuals that are both parents and offspring, which is overcome by the Bayesian update rule. In addition, genotypic error models are extended to account for sequencing errors such as allelic bias and overdispersion in genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS). Extensive simulations were used to compare PolyOrigin2 with previous methods and to study the effects of such variables as sequencing errors and the number of progeny per parent. We further evaluated PolyOrigin2 using three real datasets: diploid potato with 23 founders and 7 generations, tetraploid potato with 10 founders and 3 generations, and tetraploid blueberry with 10 founders and 4 generations. The results show that PolyOrigin2 is accurate for haplotype phasing and reconstruction in diploid and tetraploid pedigrees and opens new opportunities for haplotype-based QTL mapping.

papers.title: PDAC BioPortal: An Integrated Web Resource for Multi-Scale Analysis of Pancreatic Cancer Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound cellular heterogeneity and treatment-associated remodeling, yet bulk, single-nucleus, and spatial transcriptomic datasets remain fragmented across separate portals. We developed PDAC BioPortal, an open-access, browser-based web resource integrating four complementary human PDAC cohorts: primary tumor versus normal pancreas (TCGA-PAAD and GTEx, n = 345), a neoadjuvant stereotactic body radiotherapy-containing bulk cohort (GSE225767, n = 55), a single-nucleus chemoradiotherapy atlas (GSE202051, 224,988 nuclei across 43 patients), and 10x Genomics Visium spatial transcriptomics (GSE274103, 23,436 spots across five tumors). The platform provides interactive differential expression, rank-based pathway enrichment, patient-level pseudobulk comparisons, survival exploration, and spatial visualization, alongside PDACopilot, a deterministic, evidence-grounded natural-language query interface. Across cohorts, neoadjuvant-treated bulk and single-nucleus pathway rankings showed significant concordance, while Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition and compositional sensitivity testing separated epithelial debulking from cell-intrinsic signaling shifts. Interrogation of the NRF2-associated redox network illustrated how bulk changes diverge from cell-type-resolved and spatial patterns, while continuous Cox modeling linked higher NRF2-signature expression to shorter overall survival. PDAC BioPortal is freely available at https://limboper89.github.io/PAAD-SBRT-GEx-Dashboard/. Availability: https://limboper89.github.io/PAAD-SBRT-GEx-Dashboard/

papers.title: AIO Part I: Interpretable ADMET Prediction for Cyclic Peptides and Macrocycles
papers.abstract: Macrocycles and cyclic peptides are increasingly important in beyond-rule-of-five (bRo5) drug discovery, yet their absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties remain difficult to predict owing to sparse data, complex topology, and environment-dependent conformations. Here, we present AIO (All-in-One), an interpretable multimodal ADMET framework combining topology-preserving molecular segmentation with solvent-aware contrastive pretraining. Across repeated cross-validation, AIO performed strongly across permeability, solubility, unbound fraction, clearance, half-life, bioavailability, and toxicity endpoints, achieving Pearson R = 0.87 for PAMPA permeability and AUROC = 0.91 for bioavailability. Case studies of recently approved macrocyclic and cyclic-peptide drugs showed agreement between predictions and reported pharmacokinetic profiles, while segment-level attribution highlighted molecular regions associated with predicted ADMET bottlenecks. Despite pretraining exclusively on macrocycles, AIO also transferred competitively to the small-molecule PharmaBench dataset. These results establish a promising foundation for interpretable ADMET prediction across diverse molecular modalities in drug discovery.

papers.title: MitoArc: A Reproducible Short-Read Workflow for Human Mitochondrial Genome Analysis with Circular-Coordinate and NUMT-Aware Evaluation
papers.abstract: Human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis from short-read sequencing is complicated by nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), circular-reference coordinates, sequencing depth, and variant-caller configuration. We developed MitoArc, a Nextflow workflow that accepts paired-end FASTQ files or pre-aligned BAM and CRAM files, retains available nuclear mapping context, and performs standard and shifted-coordinate processing. It runs Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) Mutect2 and mutserve2 independently and reports mitochondrial quality metrics, NUMT evidence, haplogroups, contamination estimates, functional annotations, consensus sequences, and reproducibility outputs. We evaluated MitoArc using 18 controlled datasets, spanning three technical replicates and six sequencing depths (100x-5000x), with 648 allele-level truth observations. Requiring confident primary mitochondrial mapping eliminated 33 observable synthetic NUMT-associated false-positive calls but reduced recall from 0.894 to 0.796. In a matched evaluation comprising 108 truth observations, standard-only and standard-plus-shifted GATK processing produced identical variant recovery and allele-fraction estimates. GATK recall increased from 0.741 at 100x to 0.917 at 5000x, while temporary working storage increased approximately 20-fold. Against the complete truth set, GATK recovered 548 observations and mutserve2 recovered 311 under the evaluated configurations; mutserve2 insertion and deletion modes were not enabled. The benchmark used synthetic data without a background sequencing-error model. A reduced HG002 dataset demonstrated end-to-end operation of the pre-aligned workflow, subject to incomplete nuclear context. MitoArc preserves caller-specific evidence and the analytical context needed to interpret mitochondrial variants. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/sarvezh1/mitoarc.

papers.title: Causal regulators of human T-cell and macrophage activation from perturbation screens, and a replicated coupling of T-cell exhaustion markers with macrophage M1 activation in patients under checkpoint blockade
papers.abstract: Engineering anti-tumour immunity requires knowing which genes control T-cell and macrophage programs, and how the two compartments relate to each other in patients. We built ImmunoTwin, an analysis framework that addresses both questions with public data and with every test, baseline and criterion fixed before the result was computed. From a genome-scale CRISPR-interference Perturb-seq in primary human CD4+ T cells (22 million cells, four donors) we derive a map of regulators of the cytotoxic effector program that is calibrated, reverses direction under CRISPR activation (rho = -0.53), and tracks interferon-gamma production among the hits of independent sorting-based screens (rho = 0.69). From a Perturb-seq in primary human macrophages we recover the TLR4-NF-kappaB pathway as regulator of the lipopolysaccharide response (pathway-level P = 0.0004) and find that transcriptional effects track TNF protein measured in independent donors (rho = 0.58). In both cell types, however, a generic measure of perturbation strength recovers the hits of functional screens better than the program-specific effect (area under the ROC curve 0.96 versus 0.73 in T cells; 0.87 versus 0.72 in macrophages). In 90 patients from seven cohorts with tumour sampled before and during checkpoint blockade, T-cell and macrophage programs shifted together, most strongly T-cell exhaustion markers and the macrophage M1 program (r = 0.43). Fixed as a hypothesis and tested once in 86 further patients from six cohorts, this association replicated (r = 0.51, permutation P = 0.0001) and was specific against expression-matched random gene sets (P = 0.004). The baseline state of one compartment did not improve the forecast of the other, so the criterion we had set for calling the framework a patient-level digital twin was not met. ImmunoTwin provides two validated perturbation maps, a replicated cross-compartment association in patients, and a caution on how such maps are benchmarked.

papers.title: Prediction and Dissection of Nitrogenase Activity Based on Protein Sequences using Dual Descriptor
papers.abstract: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, but its activity differs markedly among natural sequences, and conventional wet-laboratory screening suffers from low throughput and long turnaround times. Existing computational methods have partially alleviated this bottleneck, yet most of them rely on protein embeddings obtained from protein language models together with features such as gene expression, and their interpretability analyses mostly stop at the level of feature contribution. Here we present CarmnaDD, a purely sequence-driven framework built on the dual descriptor (DD): two learnable components, the composition weight map (CWM) and the position weight function (PWF), jointly generate a position-resolved description N(k), so that activity can be predicted without any prior knowledge beyond the sequence. On the same dataset used by Carmna, CarmnaDD attains R2 = 0.60 for regression and AUC = 0.94 and F1 = 0.86 for classification, better than our previous Carmna, which integrates multiple features. Interpretability analysis shows that the amplitude of the periodic terms of the PWF decreases as the rank increases, indicating that the positional encoding strategy adapts to the rank; the high-weight 3-mer fragments in the CWM are significantly enriched in polar uncharged residues, which corroborates the SHAP-based conclusion of Carmna; sliding-window scanning identifies fragments significantly associated with activity (FDR < 0.05), and the strongest window displays a D-X-E pattern with conserved flanks and a polymorphic center, sequences carrying R at the central position showing the highest activity; conservation is significantly negatively correlated ({rho} = -0.30) with description intensity. Mapping the key windows onto the protein structure shows that four highly correlated windows converge on the nucleotide-binding interface and the conformational-transmission/protein-docking interface of NifH. These results provide a purely sequence-based framework for nitrogenase activity prediction that balances performance and interpretability.

papers.title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy for Quantitative Prediction of Multicomponent Mixtures
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML)-assisted Raman spectroscopy that can efficiently analyze molecularly specific fingerprints is well suited for quantitative analysis of complex chemical mixtures. However, developing accurate predictive ML models for multicomponent systems remains difficult because collecting sufficient experimental calibration data is slow, expensive, and limited. In this work, we present a ML-assisted Raman spectroscopy framework for predicting the quantitative composition of multicomponent lipid mixtures (consisting of 15 lipids). To reduce the experimental burden of generating extensive multicomponent spectral datasets, we computationally constructed a large spectral library using experimentally measured pure-component Raman spectra from 15 lipids, including triglycerides, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, and fatty acid methyl and ethyl esters. Mixture compositions were sampled across a constrained compositional space and used to generate training spectra from weighted combinations of the pure component spectra. Experimentally prepared mixtures were then used to evaluate the model under real measurement conditions. To reduce the mismatch between library-generated spectra and experimental mixture spectra, a linear correction strategy was applied to account for systematic spectral differences caused by mixing effects, intermolecular interactions, and measurement variability. The corrected experimental spectra were then used for concentration prediction with an uncertainty-aware workflow. The compositions of the 15 lipid mixtures were successfully predicted using the ML model trained solely on a simulated dataset, achieving R^2 values exceeding 0.95 for each lipid. By combining scalable, library-based model training with experimental validation on physical multicomponent mixtures, this approach minimizes the need for exhaustive calibration datasets while maintaining high quantitative accuracy. The proposed framework offers a practical path for quantitative Raman analysis of chemical mixtures and can easily be extended to quality control applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and chemical industries.

papers.title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
papers.abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

papers.title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

papers.title: Fragment anchoring for metabolite annotation beyond whole-spectrum similarity
papers.abstract: Many untargeted metabolomics features remain unannotated, and chemically related metabolites can have dissimilar tandem mass spectra. We present ANCHor, a framework for interpreting features of interest using shared fragment evidence. ANCHor selects fragments of a feature that recur among similar atlas spectra but are rare in background spectra, then evaluates matching experimental features using mass differences and transformation rules. Using 1,021 authentic standards as features of interest, ANCHor generated at least one anchor for 76.9%. We tested whether L-methionine anchors retain related spectra despite low overall similarity. Of 166 structurally related spectra, ANCHor retained 147, including 93 with modified cosine similarity <0.70 to L-methionine. In mycotoxin-treated hepatic spheroids, ANCHor prioritized putative transformation products, including low-similarity candidates. For library-unmatched fecal features in alcohol-associated liver disease, ANCHor found annotated references that guided identification of N1,N12-diacetylspermine, confirmed with an authentic standard, and supported a tryptophan-pyruvate product hypothesis with a reaction-generated reference. ANCHor thus supports testable structural hypotheses for library-unmatched features within atlas coverage.

papers.title: RapidGLM: genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and eQTL analysis
papers.abstract: Genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and expression QTL analyses fit millions of count regressions and estimate p-values from billions of random draws. RapidGLM, a C++ library, makes both steps fast, with Newton fits specialized to count models and draws made in batches. Its DESeq2, edgeR, SCEPTRE and cis-QTL analyses agree with the reference tools and run 2.5-17.8 times faster on the same cores. On one compute node, a CRISPR screen's 28.0 million tests took SCEPTRE 11.6 hours and RapidGLM 44 minutes, or 2.8 hours with more accurate small p-values. RapidGLM is MIT-licensed, with C, Python, R and command-line interfaces.

papers.title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
papers.abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

papers.title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
papers.abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

papers.title: Integrating disease and protein networks expands genetic support for therapeutic targets
papers.abstract: Human genetics guides therapeutic target selection, but direct genetic support covers few clinically investigated target-indication pairs, each linking a target to a disease. Here we introduce BRIDGE (Biological Relation-Informed Diffusion of Genetic Evidence), which propagates genetic evidence through coupled protein-protein interaction and disease-similarity networks. Each candidate's score is calibrated against scores obtained after randomly substituting similarly connected genes for genes with direct genetic support. In a retrospective benchmark of 13,022 pairs that had reached at least phase I, BRIDGE supported 572 additional pairs, increasing coverage from 5.1% to 9.5%. Among eligible pairs lacking direct genetic support, 25.3% of network-added pairs had reached launch versus 8.6% of remaining candidates (relative success, 2.94; 95% confidence interval, 2.51-3.45). This enrichment extended to 158 pairs involving 101 genes with no direct genetic support in the benchmark. At a matched selection size of 1,310 pairs, BRIDGE ranking captured 265 launched pairs, compared with 223 under a rule transferring support across neighbouring targets or indications. These findings show that coupling disease relationships with protein connectivity expands the reach of human genetics to additional therapeutic targets and indications while retaining clinical relevance.
